Esperanto is a planned auxiliary language created in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Polish-Jewish ophthalmologist whose utopian vision was to foster international peace and understanding through a shared neutral language. Though it never became an official international language adopted by governments, it stands as the most successful constructed language in history, with hundreds of thousands of speakers around the world. The language was designed with simplified phonetics using only regular sounds with no irregularities, combined with agglutinative morphology where words are built transparently from roots and affixes, and a completely regular grammar system with absolutely no exceptions to its rules. Depending on how fluency is measured, Esperanto has between 100,000 and 2 million speakers worldwide. Enthusiasts gather annually at international conventions to celebrate and sustain the language community. The vocabulary base draws from major European languages, primarily Romance, Germanic, and some Slavic roots, chosen to maximize intelligibility for speakers from different linguistic backgrounds. An entire Esperanto movement grew up around the language as a peace-advocacy community, with members producing literature, music, radio broadcasts, and maintaining active forums online. The movement demonstrates how even an engineered language can birth a real cultural and social movement. Although Esperanto never achieved the political adoption Zamenhof had hoped for, it successfully established itself as a thriving subculture with its own distinct identity and cultural institutions.
